lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you met the Aztecs and Incas. What were the Aztecs' floating gardens called? (Chinampas.) Today: what happened when Europe and the Americas met after 1492, told with respect.

In 1492 the Americas were home to many millions of people, speaking hundreds of languages. There were great cities and small villages: the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan, the Inca capital Cusco, the Taino of the Caribbean islands, and many more nations.

After 1492, ships carried plants, animals and people both ways across the Atlantic. Historians call this the Columbian exchange. Potatoes, maize, tomatoes and cacao went out to the world; wheat, horses, cattle and sugar cane came in.

The exchange changed the world's food. Potatoes and maize fed growing numbers of people in Europe, Africa and Asia. Tomatoes reached Italy, chilli peppers reached India and Thailand, and horses changed life on the American plains.

Diseases crossed too. Smallpox, measles and flu came from Europe, and the peoples of the Americas had never met them. In the century after 1492 a great many people died of them, in some places most of the people: one of history's worst disasters.

Spanish soldiers led by Cortés took the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, in 1521. Other nations who opposed the Aztecs helped them, and so did disease. Pizarro's soldiers took the Inca Empire in the 1530s. Spain and Portugal claimed the land, its silver and gold.

Many Indigenous people were forced to work for the new rulers; the priest Bartolomé de las Casas spoke out against it. Yet they resisted and survived: millions speak Quechua, Nahuatl or Guarani today. Grade 8 tells how Africans were enslaved in the Americas.
Try it in the world: build a market with two stalls: foods first grown in the Americas, and foods from Europe, Africa and Asia, with a sign saying who first grew them. Next: the Ottoman Empire.

exercises.prompt: What do historians call the crossing of plants, animals and diseases after 1492?
exercises.hint: It is named after the sailor of 1492.

exercises.prompt: Which of these first grew in the Americas?
exercises.hint: Think of the Andes, where the Incas farmed.
exercises.explain: Potatoes, first grown in the Andes; wheat, rice and coffee came from Europe, Africa and Asia.

exercises.prompt: Which animal was brought to the Americas from Europe?
exercises.hint: Which animal changed life on the American plains?
exercises.explain: Horses: there were none in the Americas in 1492.

exercises.prompt: In 1492 the Americas were almost empty of people.
exercises.hint: Remember Tenochtitlan and the Inca roads.
exercises.explain: False: many millions of people lived there, in cities and villages.

exercises.prompt: Which city did Cortés's soldiers take in 1521?
exercises.hint: It was the Aztec capital on a lake.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: which way did they cross the Atlantic after 1492?
exercises.hint: Think where each first grew or lived.
exercises.explain: From the Americas: potatoes, cacao, tomatoes. To the Americas: wheat, horses, sugar cane.

exercises.prompt: Why did diseases such as smallpox hit the peoples of the Americas so hard?
exercises.hint: Bodies learn to fight diseases they have met before.
choices: they had never met these diseases before
exercises.explain: They had never met these diseases, so their bodies had no defence against them.

exercises.prompt: Tenochtitlan was founded about 1325 and taken in 1521. For about how many years was it the Aztecs' city?
exercises.hint: Take the earlier year from the later one.

exercises.prompt: Who spoke out against the cruel treatment of Indigenous people?
Match each name to what it is.
exercises.hint: Three are languages still spoken; one is a people Columbus met.
exercises.explain: Quechua: the Andes. Nahuatl: Mexico. Guarani: Paraguay. Taino: the Caribbean.

exercises.prompt: How did potatoes and maize change the world?
exercises.hint: Think of food crops that grow well and feed many.
choices: they fed more people in Europe, Africa and Asia
they were only used as decoration
they were eaten only in Spain
exercises.explain: They became staple foods in Europe, Africa and Asia and helped feed growing numbers of people.

exercises.prompt: Every European of the time thought the conquest was right.
exercises.explain: False: some Europeans, such as de las Casas, spoke out against the cruelty.

exercises.prompt: Why is it important to tell this history from Indigenous people's side too?
choices: to understand what it meant for the people there
exercises.explain: History is fairer and truer when we know what happened to everyone, above all those who lived there.

exercises.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
exercises.hint: The smaller the year, the earlier.
items: Spain and Portugal split the world (1494)

exercises.prompt: Columbus arrived in 1492, and smallpox reached Mexico in 1520. How many years later?
exercises.hint: Take the earlier year from the later one.
